On paper, IELTS Listening gives you 10 extra minutes at the end to copy your answers onto the answer sheet.

On the computer, it doesn't. You type each answer into the box while you listen, and at the end you get only 2 minutes to check.

The timer keeps running the whole time, even between parts. So don't plan to "fix it later". Answer as you go, and use the pauses between parts to read the next questions.

Save this post for your next practice test.

Three 7s and one 5. What is your overall band? Your overall band is the average of your four sections, rounded to the nearest half band. Listening 7.0 Reading 7.0 Speaking 7.0 Writing 5.0 (7 + 7 + 7 + 5) ÷ 4 = 6.5 With Writing at 7.0, you would get 7.0. One weak section cost you half a band. Raise Writing to 6.0, and the average is 6.75, which rounds up to 7.0. Find your weakest section and fix it first. Which section would you raise first? posts.script:
Half an answer, half a band.
Look at this Task 2 question: "Discuss both views and give your own opinion."
That is three jobs, not one.
View one. View two. Your opinion.
Many students write a great essay about one view and forget the rest.
If you skip one part, you can't get a 6 for Task Response.
Even with perfect grammar.
So before you write, underline every instruction in the question.
After each paragraph, ask yourself: which part does this answer?
Save this and check your next essay.
posts.caption:
Half an answer, half a band.

"Discuss both views and give your own opinion" is three tasks in one question: view one, view two and your opinion.

If your essay skips one of them, Task Response can't reach a 6, even if your grammar is excellent.

Before you write, underline every instruction. After each paragraph, ask yourself: which part of the question does this answer?

Save this and use it on your next Task 2.

In IELTS Listening, the gap between band 6.0 and band 7.0 is only about 7 answers.

Roughly, 23 correct answers out of 40 give you 6.0, and 30 out of 40 give you 7.0. The exact table can change slightly from test to test, but the gap stays small.

Many of those answers are lost to small things: a spelling mistake, a missing plural "s", or more words than the question allows.

After your next practice test, don't just count your score. Look at every wrong answer and write down why you lost it.

You start Writing Task 2 almost two hours into the exam. In computer-delivered IELTS, you take Listening, Reading and Writing in one sitting, with no break between them: 🎧 Listening: about 30 minutes 📖 Reading: 60 minutes ✍️ Writing: 60 minutes By Task 2, your brain is already tired. If you only practise Writing when you feel fresh, exam day will feel much harder. Do at least one practice test in one sitting, in this order, with a timer. Then you will know how much energy you really have left for Writing. Save this post for your next practice weekend.
